outline: Hemophilia/factor VIII disorders and coagulation inhibitors
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
diagnosis: Acquired hemophilia A due to a factor VIII inhibitor
mechanism: Acquired hemophilia A results from an autoantibody that inhibits factor VIII. It should be suspected in a patient with new-onset bleeding and an isolated prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time. A factor deficiency is corrected by mixing patient plasma with normal plasma, whereas a clinically significant inhibitor prevents correction; factor VIII activity is reduced in acquired hemophilia A.
vignette: A 72-year-old woman with no personal or family history of abnormal bleeding develops spontaneous extensive ecchymoses and a large soft-tissue hematoma. Platelet count is normal. Prothrombin time is normal, but activated partial thromboplastin time is prolonged. After her plasma is mixed with an equal volume of normal plasma and incubated, the activated partial thromboplastin time remains prolonged. Factor VIII activity is markedly reduced, and testing for a lupus anticoagulant is negative.
lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correct: Acquired hemophilia A due to a factor VIII inhibitor
distractor_notes: Congenital hemophilia A is an inherited factor VIII deficiency. A simple factor deficiency generally corrects when normal plasma supplies the missing factor in a mixing study; the new-onset bleeding and failure to correct instead indicate an inhibitor.

A lupus anticoagulant can prolong the aPTT and can cause failure of correction in a mixing study, but the specific lupus-anticoagulant test is negative and the combination of bleeding with markedly reduced factor VIII activity is more consistent with a factor VIII inhibitor.

Von Willebrand disease can reduce factor VIII activity because von Willebrand factor stabilizes factor VIII, but as a deficiency pattern it should generally show correction on a mixing study rather than persistent inhibition after incubation.
Factor XI deficiency can prolong the aPTT and cause bleeding, but normal plasma supplies factor XI and should correct a deficiency pattern in a mixing study.
key_expl: This patient has acquired hemophilia A. The defining mechanism is an acquired inhibitor, usually an autoantibody, against factor VIII. The new onset of spontaneous soft-tissue bleeding in a person without a prior bleeding history, normal PT and platelet count, isolated prolonged aPTT, low factor VIII activity, and failure of an incubated mixing study to correct the aPTT together indicate a factor VIII inhibitor rather than an inherited factor deficiency.
objective: Recognize acquired hemophilia A when new-onset bleeding is accompanied by isolated aPTT prolongation, reduced factor VIII activity, and failure of an incubated mixing study to correct, indicating a factor VIII inhibitor.
clues: mixing study fails to correct after incubation

sources.organization: National Library of Medicine / PubMed Central
sources.title: International recommendations on the diagnosis and treatment of patients with acquired hemophilia A
sources.support: International recommendations state that acquired hemophilia A should be considered with acute/recent bleeding and unexplained prolonged aPTT and explain that factor VIII inhibitors are time- and temperature-dependent, making incubated mixing studies useful for distinguishing inhibitors from factor deficiencies.

sources.organization: National Library of Medicine / PubMed Central
sources.title: Consensus recommendations for the diagnosis and treatment of acquired hemophilia A
sources.support: The consensus review explains that normal plasma corrects aPTT caused by factor deficiency, whereas a factor VIII inhibitor prevents correction; incubation is important because factor VIII inhibitors can be time dependent.
